source.title: Training Deep Spiking Neural Networks
source.authors: Eimantas Ledinauskas; J. Ruseckas; Alfonsas Jursenas; Giedrius Burachas

record.tranche_reason: Tests gradient training, depth scaling, and batch normalization in spiking neural networks, a different network type from the versions’ main examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own CIFAR100 training-accuracy depth sweep and CIFAR10 training-loss curves with and without batch normalization. It does not report random-label training, shortcut-versus-plain comparisons, or results for the other versions’ specified initializations or learning-rate mechanisms.
record.test_reason: The controlled batch-normalization comparison tests V6 in a new setting: a ResNet18 spiking neural network. The surrogate-gradient depth experiments do not directly test the conventional-network training claims in V1 or V3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that tuning surrogate-gradient width addresses exploding and vanishing gradients and input-current batch normalization accelerates SNN training, enabling direct ResNet50 training. Depth scaling remains problematic even with controlled gradients. They also report far fewer inference time steps than conversion methods and occasional shallow-SNN advantages over analogous ANNs.
record.recipe_differences: Direct surrogate-gradient training of integrate-and-fire spiking neural networks; SNN dynamics and surrogate gradients differ from the versions’ conventional ANN recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth affects training accuracy; surrogate-gradient width affects gradient behavior; batch normalization speeds convergence in the reported SNN learning curves; training and inference time steps affect the reported test-accuracy behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-gamma SNN training accuracy declines beginning at five layers; tuning surrogate-gradient width improves depth scaling, although performance eventually deteriorates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surrogate-gradient width controls gradient propagation and attainable training performance as spiking-network depth increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Small gamma produces exploding gradients and large gamma produces vanishing gradients in ResNet18 SNNs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surrogate-gradient choice affects gradient propagation in spiking networks; this is distinct from changing parameter initialization.

record.problems: Figure 5 provides the depth-sweep training accuracies only as plots, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The paper reports only three random initializations for the inference-time-step experiment, whose metric is test accuracy rather than training error.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying additional result rows omitted.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large conventional convolutional networks, random or corrupted labels, and controlled model-size, stopping, or regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization and the effect of extra student neurons on spurious minima.
Conventional plain-network depth degradation with longer training, matched identity-shortcut comparisons, and the stated tanh and Fixup exceptions.
Comparisons of parameter initializations, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and initialization-dependent trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss growth, curvature evolution, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Higher learning-rate tolerance, the original ANN settings, and Fixup comparisons. The fixed-rate SNN experiment establishes convergence speed only.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Remove the V1 limits_scope verdict: unreadable tuned-gamma accuracies and degradation in a different, fixed-gamma condition do not establish that verdict. Numerical values cannot be reconstructed from the supplied figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-10 near-zero training error, SGD or Adam in the version’s stated settings, and comparisons with smaller models or early stopping are not tested.
The paper examines depth scaling in SNNs, but does not compare the same networks with and without identity shortcuts or show that shortcuts prevent the reported degradation.
The tests use SNNs, not the version’s specified sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, or Inception ImageNet settings; Fixup is not tested.
